orbitModes.label: Single Landsat
orbitModes.title: Single Landsat baseline
orbitModes.description: One Landsat satellite flies in a near-polar, sun-synchronous orbit at about 705 km altitude, crossing the equator at roughly the same local morning time and revisiting the same place every 16 days.
orbitModes.caption: A single Landsat mission provides systematic global land imaging with a 16-day revisit cycle.

orbitModes.label: Landsat 8 + 9
orbitModes.title: Landsat 8 and 9 working as a pair
orbitModes.description: Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 occupy complementary phasing so they image the same location eight days apart. That near-weekly cadence is especially important for water quality, crop condition, and tropical forest monitoring.
orbitModes.caption: Two Landsat satellites, phased eight days apart, create an 8-day repeat over the same location.

orbitModes.label: HLS Constellation
orbitModes.title: HLS virtual constellation
orbitModes.description: Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 treats multiple compatible missions as one analysis-ready observing system. NASA reports a global median repeat frequency under 1.4 days in 2025 with Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2A/B/C.
orbitModes.caption: Landsat plus Sentinel-2 dramatically increases repeat observations while preserving Landsat-like analysis workflows.

resolutionModes.label: Spatial
resolutionModes.title: Spatial resolution
resolutionModes.description: Spatial resolution tells you how much ground each pixel covers. Landsat 9 offers 15 m panchromatic, 30 m visible-to-shortwave infrared, and 100 m thermal pixels, which is why it is so useful for field-to-region scale work.

cards.title: 15 m
cards.text: Sharper panchromatic detail for edges, roads, and urban structure.

cards.title: 30 m
cards.text: The core Landsat working scale for vegetation, water, land cover, and change detection.

cards.title: 100 m thermal
cards.text: Coarser heat measurements, still extremely useful for evapotranspiration and urban heat analysis.

resolutionModes.label: Spectral
resolutionModes.title: Spectral resolution
resolutionModes.description: Spectral resolution describes how many wavelength bands a sensor captures and where those bands sit in the electromagnetic spectrum. Landsat 9 carries 11 bands spanning coastal, visible, near-infrared, shortwave-infrared, panchromatic, cirrus, and thermal infrared.

cards.title: Vegetation and moisture
cards.text: NIR and SWIR support plant condition, burn severity, and surface moisture analysis.

cards.title: Water and coastlines
cards.text: Coastal and visible bands help with water quality, turbidity, and shoreline interpretation.

cards.title: Heat and energy balance
cards.text: Thermal bands make Landsat uniquely useful for water use, drought, and urban heat studies.

resolutionModes.label: Temporal
resolutionModes.title: Temporal resolution
resolutionModes.description: Temporal resolution is about how often you can observe the same place. One Landsat mission repeats every 16 days, Landsat 8 and 9 together achieve 8 days, and HLS compresses the wait dramatically by harmonizing Landsat with Sentinel-2.

facts.label: HLS
facts.value: 2 to 3 days, < 1.4 day median globally in 2025

resolutionModes.label: Radiometric
resolutionModes.title: Radiometric resolution
resolutionModes.description: Radiometric resolution tells you how finely a sensor can distinguish differences in reflected or emitted energy. More bits means more measurable shades between dark and bright surfaces. Landsat 7 used 8-bit data, while Landsat 9 OLI collects 14-bit data.
resolutionModes.story: Higher radiometric precision helps scientists detect subtler differences in dark vegetation, bright soils, snow, and water while preserving strong time-series comparability.
